questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{x-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{3}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{x-1}\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =3\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4{e}^{2x}=-2x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{2x}-2x.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}y & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)+6{x}^{2}=4x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =4x-6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4x-6{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =4\int x\,\text{d}x-6\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{3} \\  & =2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}+C \\  & =2{x}^{2}(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
questions.problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\sqrt{x}=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\sqrt{x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(\frac{2}{5}\,{x}^{5/2})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{4}{15}\,{x}^{5/2}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
questions.problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+5=6{x}^{2}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=6{x}^{2}-5.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (6{x}^{2}-5)\text{d}x \\  & =6\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-5\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-5x+C \\  & =2{x}^{3}-5x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}-5x+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =2\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-5\int x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =2(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})-5(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{2}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition
questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}-2x={e}^{x/2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{y}^{′}=2x+{e}^{x/2}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x/2})\text{d}x \\ y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2{e}^{x/2}+C \\  & ={x}^{2}+2{e}^{x/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y={x}^{2}+2{e}^{x/2}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(0)=2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & ={0}^{2}+2{e}^{0}+C \\ 2 & =0+2(1)+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y={x}^{2}+2{e}^{x/2}.
$$

$$

$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,\text{d}x \\ y & =4\int (x+1)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4(2(x+1)^{1/2})+C \\  & =8\sqrt{x+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=8\sqrt{x+1}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(3)=10$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =8\sqrt{3+1}+C \\ 10 & =8(2)+C \\ C & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=8\sqrt{x+1}-6.
$$

questions.problem: Find the specific solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4=0$ given that $y(-1)=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int (-4)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-4x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=-4x+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(-1)=4$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =-4\cdot (-1)+C \\ 4 & =4+C \\ 0 & =C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=-4x\,.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${f}^{′}(x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ that satisfies the condition $f(0)=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =-2\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0)=-1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡0+C \\ -1 & =-2(0)+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
f(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${f}^{′}(x)-4x=1$ that satisfies the condition $f(1)=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=4x+1.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =4\int x\,\text{d}x+\int \text{d}x \\  & =4(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+x+C \\  & =2{x}^{2}+x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(1)=-1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =2(1)^{2}+1+C \\ -1 & =2+1+C \\ C & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x-4.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition $f(0)=2.$

$$
f'(x) - \dfrac{3}{1+x^2} = 0
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac{3}{1+x^2}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =3\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $f(x) = 3\arctan{x} + C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0) = 2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ 2 & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is 

$$
f(x)=3\arctan x + 2.
$$
